title: Apps to work with HMT data sets
text: Since these apps are self-contained HTML pages, you can download them and use them on your own computer, or follow the links below to use the current version installed on github pages.

Facsmile views

Venetus A facsimile: browse page images of the Venetus A, hover over indexed page to see textual edition

title: Apps to work with HMT data sets
text:
Text-oriented apps

Iliad + scholia reader: select passage of the Iliad and view any scholia on the selected lines
Cross-manuscript scholia reader: select passage of the Iliad in a given version, and view passage together with scholia from all edited versions
Simple text search: search text of Iliad and scholia for strings of text.
Count results of string search: search text of Iliad and scholia for strings of text, tabulate frequencies, optionally explore individual passages.
Find texts by proper names: find occurrences of personal, geographic and ethnic names and see their text in context.
Interwoven diplomatic/normalized reader: read Iliad and scholia texts in diplomatic transcription with editorial normalizations in parentheses.

title: Where should I start?
text:
The HMT archive is large and complex. Rather than try to produce a comprehensive HMT app, I am experimenting with numerous small, focused apps. The list of currently running apps has grown to the point it might not be obvious how to get started. Here are some suggestions.

if you want to browse the HMT project’s collection of manuscripts images: try images.html
if you want to read editions of the Iliad and scholia: try iliad-scholia.html
if you want a fascimile view of our most completely edited manuscript, the Venetus A: try va-facsimile.html

title: About hmt-apps
text:
Throughout the first quarter of the twenty-first century, the Homer Multitext project’s (HMT) work on Homeric manuscripts intentionally prioritized building openly licensed data sets in simple plain-text formats over developing apps. Major components of the archive include (among other things):

collections of digital images of Homeric manuscripts
cataloged data about manuscripts of the Iliad
editions of texts of the Iliad and scholia
indexes associating texts, manuscript pages, and images
other indexes including proper nouns and adjectives

This fundamental decision about how to distribute its work is epitomized in the publication of the HMT archive in a single plain-text file, that is always available in its most recent release on github, here.

title: About hmt-apps
text:
“Two-coffee apps”
This repository is a personal project inspired by the potential of coding agents like Claude. Working with the HMT project’s data releases constantly inspires new ideas for apps to explore the complex interrelationships in the HMT data. With an agentic assistant, it’s straightforward to try these ideas out very quickly. I developed ach of the apps linked here to a point where I was comfortable releasing it on github in less time than it took me to finish two cups of coffee. The initial investment in both time and coffee is small enough that if an idea doesn’t work out, I can just throw it away without hesitation. This dramatically accelerated release cycle gives new meaning to Eric Raymond’s famous aphorism, “Release early, release often.” By reducing the effort to build an app, coding agents can be a boon to scholars with expertise in particular subject matter, rather than in software engineering.
All of the apps in this repository start by downloading the HMT project’s latest data release. Apps quickly developed by agents like Claude amplify the datasets’ value, and offer a powerful new justification for the HMT project’s decision to favor developing datasets over software.
